When you veto something, you officially and authoritatively reject or block a decision, plan, or law — stopping it from happening — even if other people have already agreed to it or voted for it.

The single most important thing to understand is this: a veto is not just a "no" from anyone. It is a powerful, formal "no" that actually kills or stops something. And only certain people, in certain roles, have the power to use it.

Imagine a group of people vote on a decision. The majority agrees. Everything seems settled. But then one specific person — someone with special authority — steps in and says, "I reject this. It will not go forward." That act of blocking it? That is a veto.

So to veto something is to:

  • Refuse to approve it, and
  • Use your authority to prevent it from taking effect.

Both parts matter. A regular person can refuse to approve something, but their refusal doesn't necessarily stop it. When someone vetoes it, their refusal does stop it — because they hold the power to do so.

In government (the most common context):

In many countries, a president or a monarch can veto a bill (a proposed law) that has been passed by the legislature (the parliament or congress). This means even though the lawmakers voted "yes," the president can step in and say "no," and the bill does not become a law.

For example: "The president vetoed the bill, so it never became a law."

In international bodies:

In the United Nations Security Council, five powerful countries (the US, UK, France, Russia, and China) each have the right to veto any major resolution. If even one of them vetoes it, the resolution is blocked — no matter how many other countries supported it.

For example: "Russia vetoed the resolution, so the Security Council could not take action."

In everyday informal use:

People also use "veto" more loosely in everyday life to mean firmly shooting down someone's idea — often humorously.

For example: "I suggested we go camping, but my wife vetoed it immediately."
Or: "The kids wanted pizza every night, but Dad vetoed that plan."

Here, the word still carries the same flavour — one person using their authority (as a spouse, a parent, a boss) to block what others wanted.
What a Veto Does NOT Mean

This is subtle but important:

  • Vetoing something does not always mean it is gone forever. In many systems, a veto can be overridden — meaning if enough people push back strongly enough (for example, a two-thirds majority in the US Congress), they can reverse the veto and make the decision stand anyway.
  • Vetoing something is not the same as simply disagreeing. You can disagree with something all you want, but you can only veto it if you have been given the formal authority to do so.
  • A veto is not a punishment. It is a mechanism — a built-in check — that gives certain people the power to block decisions they find unacceptable.

"Veto" carries a sense of finality and authority. When someone vetoes something, it lands with weight. It is decisive. It shuts a door. This is why the word is also used dramatically in casual conversation — when you veto your friend's bad idea for a road trip, you're borrowing that sense of firm, no-nonsense authority.
To veto something is to officially use your authority to reject and block it, preventing it from moving forward — regardless of who else agreed to it.
